title: Chapter 1: Dry by Morning
blurb: A night caretaker promises a tenant her kitchen wall will be dry by morning, then follows the leak to a floor that is not on any drawing.

blocks.text: At one in the morning the kitchen wall of flat 4D was running with water, and there was nothing above it.

I don't mean nothing much. Above 4D's ceiling there was the roof void, then slate, then Vellhaven's usual low orange sky. No tank. No pipe. I had traced every pipe in Pellory Court, all four storeys of it, and none of them went there.
"Sorry," I told the wall, because somebody had to say it to someone. "I'll have you dry by morning."

The wall went on running. It came down in a clean sheet from the angle of the ceiling, behind the kettle, over the tiles, and pooled along the skirting where Lou Mabbott had lined up every towel she owned.
"Not the good ones," I said. "Don't put the good ones down, Lou. It's clean water, but it'll still mark them. Have you got a bucket?"

"We've got a washing-up bowl," said Lou, pulling her dressing gown tighter. Her son Danny was asleep in the back bedroom with the door ajar. He was nine and slept through everything. I'd once watched him sleep through a fire alarm test, which I'd admired. "Is it going to come through the light?"

"I'll take that circuit off to be on the safe side." I found the fuse board in their hall cupboard, under a hoover and a bag of bags, and flipped the kitchen lights off. In the dark the water sounded louder. "Bowl under the corner, there. Good. If it fills, tip it in the sink and put it back."
"I was going to ring the Trust," said Lou.
She looked at the floor. She worked at the bakery on Mallow Street and brought me the broken loaves on Fridays. "Only because it's the emergency line, Ravi. That's what it's for."
"It is," I said. "Give me till morning."

I didn't say why. The Wickline Residential Trust paid me three hundred and eighty a week, cash, to be night superintendent of their building, and the job came with flat B1 in the basement, rent-free, which was the part that mattered. A call to the emergency line at one in the morning meant a contractor at eight, and the contractor would find whatever I couldn't, and somebody at the Trust would start wondering what I was for. I still owed eleven thousand four hundred on the Fennick Lofts settlement. Without B1 I'd owe it from a sofa.
So I went looking for the pipe.

There are four public risers in Pellory Court, one at each corner. I opened the cupboard on the fourth-floor landing first, because it was nearest to 4D, and put my hand flat on each pipe in turn, and then on the back wall. Dry. I went down to three and did the same, in case the water was somehow climbing, which water doesn't. Dry. I did the far corners. Dry, and dry.

That left the roof void. A cracked pipe up there was the obvious answer, the one I'd have written on a survey without thinking twice: some forgotten feed to some forgotten tank, split with age, draining down through the joists onto the nearest kitchen. I fetched the steps, pushed up the hatch on the landing and climbed in.
Dust. Joists. Old insulation like a grey duvet. I crawled to the corner over 4D's kitchen and put my hand on the joists, on the insulation, on the back of the ceiling plaster.
Bone dry. Warm, even.
I knelt there a while with the torch pointing at nothing. Below me, very faintly, I could hear the water running down the wall of a flat that had nothing above it but me.
When I climbed back down, the door of 4C across the landing was open on its chain, and Mrs Wrobel was watching me through the gap. She was seventy-one and had a face like a closed shop.
"Dry?" she said.
"Dry," I said.

"Hm." She looked at the dust on my knees. "You'll catch your death up there, Mr Caretaker. Go and put a jumper on." Then she shut the door, and I heard her cough on the other side of it, once, and the chain go back across.
I'd had an explanation, a good one, and the building had taken it off me.
I went down to the basement to think, because that's where the old super kept his notes.

The office is a room the size of a lift, next to the boiler room: a desk, a chair, a kettle, and the Works Book. The old super had left his notes on index cards pinned round the walls in heavy pencil capitals. NO 3 RISER BANGS IN FROST, LEAVE IT. 2A LOCK STICKS, LIFT AND TURN. DOG GETS THE END OF THE MILK. I'd found them comforting, the way a stranger's handwriting is comforting when they've plainly loved a place.
The Works Book was open.

I hadn't left it open. It was a big carbon-triplicate ledger in green cloth, the size of a paving slab, and in a hundred and twenty nights the only thing in it had been the first page: the terms of the post, written out in a neat copperplate hand, with my signature under them from the night I started, and in the margin, in the same copperplate, '380 / 410'. I'd taken that for a bookkeeping note. My wage against some budget line. Somebody at the Trust doing sums.
Now there was a second page, in the same hand, in red.
``` CARETAKER: R. ANAND GRADE: 0 CREDITS: 0 HOLDING: 0 CERTIFIED: NONE
WO-5-001 FLOOR 5. TIER 1. FAULT: LEAK. CAUSE: UNDIAGNOSED. GRADE REQUIRED: 1. SYMPTOM: WET CHILL. WATERY COUGH. STATUS: OPEN. BROKEN THROUGH TO 4D. TAKEN BY: ______________ ```

The copperplate wasn't mine. My writing looks like a fence after a storm. It wasn't the old super's either: his was all over the walls, and his was a hammer, and this was a pen held by someone with time. So there was somebody else. The old super had left a backlog of jobs, the way old supers do, and somebody with a key, somebody from the Trust, had been keeping the book from their end. Tonight they'd come in while I was up a ladder and written up the 4D leak before I'd even found it.

Floor 5 bothered me for about a second. Old buildings number their plant spaces. There'd be a drawing in a drawer at the Trust that called the roof void Level 5, and whoever kept this book worked off that drawing and not off the four storeys you could see from the street. 'Broken through to 4D' was a clerk's way of saying the leak had come down into the flat. 'Watery cough' I knew from my first job: it's what the old fitters called a pipe with air in it, one that splutters and knocks when you open a tap. 'Wet chill' was the flat, near enough.
So the job was real, and it was mine, and somebody wanted a name against it.

I read the slip twice, slowly. My lips moved. They always do. Then I took the biro off the desk, signed on the line, R. ANAND, and tore the carbon copy off along the perforations, the way you tear off a job sheet to take with you.
The cold came in as I folded it.

It settled in my chest as if I'd breathed in fog, a wet, heavy chill under the breastbone, and I coughed, and the cough had water in it. A cold coming on, I decided, and about time. Four months of nights, sleeping next to a boiler that fires up at five, kneeling in roof voids at one in the morning: you don't get away with that for ever. I put the slip in my shirt pocket and went to the service corridor.

The maintenance lift lives at the back of the building, behind a steel door only my key opens. It's a cage with a wooden floor and room for four people and a dog, and I'd used it every night to haul bins and boxes and once a sofa. The panel is brass, polished by a hundred years of thumbs. B. G. 1, 2, 3, 4. Above the 4 there's a column of round holes, a dozen or so, each one painted over in the same cream as the cage, the way you'd blank off buttons for floors that got cancelled. And at the very top, on its own, stamped into the brass, a capital P.
I'd decided on my first night that the P meant penthouse. A four-storey block on Wickline Street with a penthouse. I'd thought that was funny, and said so to Dusty, who had sighed.
Tonight the first hole above the 4 wasn't painted any more. There was a brass button in it with a little lamp behind a glass bead, and the lamp was lit. Under it, in the brass, a 5.
"Well," I said. "There it is."
I was relieved. A button for the plant level nobody had told me about: that was a thing a building could have. That was a drawing in a drawer.

Something leant against my leg. Dusty had come round from the lobby, where he slept on the mat under the post table, and was standing beside me in the cage: a scruffy grey lurcher with a beard and eyebrows and the general air of a man waiting for a bus. He'd come with the job. The tenants called him Dusty and fed him in turns, and nobody seemed to know how old he was.
"You're supposed to be on the mat," I told him. "Mrs Wrobel will think I've stolen you. Mind your feet, then."
He minded his feet. I pressed 5.

The cage went up past 4 and kept going, which it shouldn't have done, because above 4 there's a metre and a half of joists and duvet, then the motor room, then sky. It kept going for about as long as it takes to climb a floor. Then it stopped, and the doors folded back, and I looked out at a corridor.

Not a void. Not a motor room. A corridor, with brown lino and a dado rail and wallpaper the colour of weak tea, lit by bulbs in glass shades like upturned bowls. Panelled doors down both sides, numbered on little enamel plates. 5-1. 5-2. It ran away from me towards the front of the building, and it went on running after the front of the building should have stopped it.
I know how long Pellory Court is. I've measured it. That corridor was longer.
"Right," I said. "Right, then."

Dusty walked out as if he'd been doing it for years. I followed him, because I wasn't going to stand in a lift by myself talking to nobody, and the lino was solid underfoot, cold through my boots and slightly tacky, the way lino gets in a damp building.

"This isn't on any drawing," I told the dog. "I've seen every drawing of this building there is. There's no fifth floor. You can see from the street. You go out every morning and do your business against the lamp post, you've seen it, there's four floors."
Dusty sniffed the skirting.
"I'm not saying you're wrong to be calm," I said. "I'd just like to know what you know."

Somewhere ahead, water was dripping. Not running, the way it ran down 4D's wall: dripping, steady, onto something hollow. I followed it, because that was the job, and following a sound was something I knew how to do. Past 5-3. Past a door with no number at all and a smell of mushrooms coming round its edges. Behind the skirting something small went scritch, scritch, like someone sorting a pocketful of change, and stopped when I looked.
"I hear you," I said to the dripping, louder than I needed to. "I'm coming. You keep doing that and I'll find you. Don't go shy on me now."
The cough came up again and I coughed it into my elbow. The chill sat in my chest like wet washing.

The dripping led to a tall narrow door near the far end, with a brass plate that said RISER. I knew that kind of door. I had four of them. Behind it was a riser, an honest one, iron and copper going up and down through the floor in the dark, and the back wall of the cupboard was shining wet.
"Hello," I said. "There you are."

I put the torch on it and my hands on it, and the fear went somewhere I couldn't feel it, because this was a pipe and I know pipes. Cold-water riser. Somebody, decades ago, had cut out a cracked length of the original iron and dropped in a newer section, and instead of a proper joint they'd sleeved it with a rubber coupling and two hose clips and walked away whistling. Two-inch bore. The rubber had gone hard as an old eraser and crazed all over, and along one side it had split, and the water was weeping out of the seam in a sheet, down the iron, into the floor. Straight down. Straight towards the corner of 4D's kitchen, if 4D's kitchen was underneath this cupboard. Which it couldn't be. Which it was.
"Perished coupling," I told Dusty. "That's all you are," I told the coupling. "A bodge somebody did on a Friday."

There was an old crutch-handled stopcock at knee height, and when I tried it gently it moved, which was the first nice thing anyone had done for me all night. I didn't shut it yet. I had a hacksaw and grips and screwdrivers in my bag, and no spares, because I hadn't known I'd be fixing a pipe in a corridor that wasn't there.

There's a right way to do a job. You find what's wrong, you write down what you found, you fetch what you need, you fix it, and you sign it off where it is. I'd worked that way since I was nineteen. So I went back down.

In the office the Works Book was open where I'd left it, and the cause line still said UNDIAGNOSED. I wrote beside it, in my fence-after-a-storm hand, PERISHED RUBBER COUPLING ON COLD RISER, SPLIT. My writing sat next to the copperplate like a builder who's walked into a wedding.

The spares were next door in the storeroom, in a cardboard box the old super had labelled SPARES. New rubber couplings, still in their bags. I took a two-inch one and two new clips and went back to the lift, where Dusty was waiting in the cage as if he'd known I'd be back.
The 5 was still lit.

On the fifth floor I knelt in the riser cupboard and shut the stopcock. The weeping thinned to a drip, and the drip stopped. I let the length drain into my bucket, loosened the old clips, which fought me, and cut the old coupling off with a knife, because it wouldn't come any other way. It came away in my hand like rotten orange peel. The iron underneath was pitted but sound. I wiped both ends dry, eased the new coupling over the iron and the newer pipe, centred it so each went in by the same depth, and tightened the clips down a turn on one and a turn on the other until the rubber bulged a little round the bands.
Then I opened the stopcock slowly, with my face close to the joint and the torch on it.
Nothing. Not a bead. I wiped it with my thumb and waited and wiped it again. Dry.
"There," I said. "Dry by morning. I said."

The carbon slip was in my shirt pocket, damp from my chest. I unfolded it on my knee. At the bottom, under the line I'd signed in the office, there was another line I hadn't paid attention to: SIGNED OFF AT FAULT. I'd have signed it here anyway; it's where you sign a job off. I signed it, R. ANAND, against the cupboard door.
The cold went out of my chest.

Not slowly, the way a cold eases. All at once, like a hand lifted off. One moment there was wet washing under my ribs and the next there was plain dry air, and I breathed in all the way to the bottom and didn't cough.
I stayed kneeling there for a bit.
"Huh," I said.
Dusty was sitting in the corridor watching me with his head on one side.

I wanted to see 4D. I'd promised that wall, and I wanted to see it with my own eyes. I left my bag where it was, ran for the lift and pressed G. Dusty didn't come. He sat on the lino as the doors folded shut, which I noticed and didn't have time for.
In 4D the hall lamp was on, and Lou opened the door before I'd knocked.
"It stopped," she said. "Ten minutes ago. It was going, and then it was going less, and then it wasn't. What was it?"
"A coupling upstairs," I said. "It's done."

"The roof, then," said Lou, nodding, as if she'd thought so all along, and I let her have the roof. The wall was still dark with wet, but nothing was coming down it, and nothing was landing in the bowl. I told her to leave the kitchen lights off till it had dried out and I'd come and put them back on at eight. Through the bedroom door I could see Danny, flat on his back with one arm off the bed, still asleep. Lou handed me a slice of banana bread wrapped in kitchen roll, and I didn't argue, because I never do. I ate it by the wet wall and said thank you more times than anyone needed. It was ten to four. Morning was a long way off.
Then I went down to the office and stood in the doorway and looked at the Works Book.
``` CARETAKER: R. ANAND GRADE: 0 CREDITS: 1 HOLDING: 0 CERTIFIED: NONE
WO-5-001 FLOOR 5. TIER 1. FAULT: LEAK. CAUSE: PERISHED RUBBER COUPLING ON COLD RISER, SPLIT. GRADE REQUIRED: 1. SYMPTOM: WET CHILL. WATERY COUGH. STATUS: CLOSED. TAKEN BY: R. ANAND ```
The whole entry had gone from red to black: the copperplate, my scrawl in the cause line, my signature. The header said CREDITS: 1, and HOLDING: 0.

Somebody from the Trust might have a key to this office. Nobody from the Trust could have known the moment I signed a slip on my knees in a cupboard on a floor that wasn't there. The entry had gone black because I'd signed it off. The book had done it, or the building had.

And the cold hadn't been a cold. It had come when I signed under TAKEN BY and gone when I signed under SIGNED OFF AT FAULT, and in between it had been exactly what the slip said: a wet chill and a watery cough, the leak's own trouble sitting in my chest. The book hadn't been describing 4D. It had been describing me. Signing for a job here didn't just mean doing it. It meant carrying it until it was done.
"Huh," I said again, to nobody, because the dog was upstairs.
The dog was upstairs. On a floor that wasn't there. With my bag.

I went back to the lift. The 5 was still lit. I'd half expected it to be painted over again, but there it was, a little lamp behind a glass bead, and when I pressed it the cage went up past 4 and on for the length of a floor, and the doors folded back on the tea-coloured corridor.
Dusty was sitting exactly where I'd left him.

"Come on, then," I told him, walking past him to the riser cupboard. "I wasn't going to leave you. I just had to look at a wall. You'd have done the same." I picked up the bag. The coupling was still dry. I put my hand on it anyway, the way you'd pat a horse. "Good. You stay like that."

The corridor was very quiet now the dripping had stopped. Behind the skirting something went scritch, once, and thought better of it. I walked back up the lino with the bag on my shoulder, talking the whole way, mostly to the dog, about how I'd redo that riser properly in daylight, a real joint, none of this rubber, and how I'd look at the drawings in the morning, and how there'd be a sensible reason, because there's always a sensible reason in a building if you're patient enough to find it.
I stepped into the cage. Dusty stepped in after me and sat down by my boots, and I turned to press G.

The doors were still open on the fifth floor, the bulbs lit all the way down. And the dog looked up at me from under his old grey eyebrows, opened his mouth, and spoke in a gravelly, unhurried voice, like a working man at the end of a long shift.
"You signed it. Good. Don't sign anything else till I've explained."
